sections.heading: Coming to you with my real sins
sections.text: Holy Lord, I come to you honestly. I have sinned more times than I can count. Pride and unbelief still show up in me. I have opened your Word without really wanting your mind. I have moved through ordinary days without looking for you or depending on you. My sins and failures could name charge after charge against me, and I have no excuse to offer.
theological_themes: Confession of repeated sin before a holy God
Specific acknowledgment of pride, unbelief, neglect of Scripture, and prayerlessness
Refusal to minimize guilt or hide behind excuses

scripture_references.connection: David’s confession treats sin first as an offense against God, not merely as personal failure or social harm. This supports the prayer’s direct honesty before the holy Lord.

This passage presents God’s Word as exposing the heart before the God to whom all must give account. It connects with the confession of failing to seek God’s mind in Scripture and standing uncovered before him.

sections.heading: Resting my case on Christ
sections.text: But I thank you that these accusations will not have the final word over me. You have laid my sin on Christ. He has carried what I could never answer for, and because of him I do not have to pretend I am innocent in order to come near to you.
theological_themes: Christ bears the guilt of sinners
Forgiveness rests on Christ’s atoning work, not self-defense
Freedom to confess because condemnation has been dealt with in Christ

scripture_references.connection: Isaiah describes the Servant bearing the iniquity of God’s people, which directly grounds the prayer’s confidence that sin has been laid on Christ rather than left on the believer.

Paul explains that there is no condemnation for those in Christ because God dealt with sin in his Son. This supports the prayer’s assurance that the accusations of sin will not stand against the believer.

sections.heading: Asking you to rule what still fights in me
sections.text: Please keep going after the corruption that still lives in me. Give me grace not to be mastered by it. Do not let the cravings of my body or the restless desires of my mind take control of my soul. Rule me yourself—with the freedom and power that come from belonging to you.
theological_themes: Conflict with fleshly desires and disordered thoughts
God’s rule brings true freedom rather than bondage

scripture_references.connection: Paul commands believers not to let sin reign in their mortal bodies and grounds that call in grace. This fits the prayer’s request not to be mastered by sinful desires but ruled by God.
This passage names the conflict between the desires of the flesh and the Spirit. It supports the prayer’s plea for God to govern the inner life where competing desires are active.

sections.heading: Thanking you for saying no when my prayers were wrong
sections.text: Thank you for the prayers you have refused. I have asked for things from selfish motives. I have wanted comfort that would have pulled me backward into slavery. I have wanted Egypt, and you have given me the wilderness instead. Please keep doing your patient work in me. When my prayers are wrong, say no. And when you say no, make me willing to receive it from your hand.
theological_themes: God’s loving refusal of selfish or spiritually harmful prayers
Submission to God’s wisdom in unanswered prayer
The wilderness as painful mercy when old bondage looks attractive

scripture_references.connection: James teaches that some prayers are not granted because they arise from disordered desires. This directly supports the confession that some requests were rightly refused because they were asked wrongly.

Israel’s longing for Egypt in the wilderness shows how God’s people can prefer familiar bondage to the hard road of deliverance. The prayer uses that biblical pattern to confess misplaced desires for comfort or return.

sections.heading: Trusting your discipline when it burns away what is false
sections.text: Cleanse me from false desires, low ambitions, and anything that resists your rule. Thank you for your wisdom and love, even in discipline. When you put me through fire, do it to refine what is precious and burn away what is worthless. The hardest burden is not pain itself, but seeing my sin clearly. If I had to choose between an easy life that leaves my sin untouched and suffering that you use to make me holy, give me the suffering that is sanctified by your hand.
theological_themes: God’s fatherly discipline is wise and loving
Trials can refine faith and expose sin
Holiness is better than comfort when comfort preserves sin

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews presents God’s discipline as the loving training of a Father who aims at holiness and righteousness in his children. This grounds the prayer’s gratitude for discipline even when it is painful.
Peter compares tested faith to gold refined by fire. This supports the image of trial as a furnace that removes dross and proves what God has made precious.

sections.heading: Free me to delight in you and walk uprightly
sections.text: Deliver me from every evil habit, every layer of old sin that has hardened around me, and everything that dulls the brightness of your grace in my life. Remove whatever keeps me from taking real delight in you. Then I will bless you, the God who helps your people walk uprightly, because any integrity in me will be your gift.
theological_themes: Deliverance from ingrained patterns of sin
Grace becoming visible in a changed life
Delight in God as the goal of cleansing and sanctification
Uprightness as God’s work in the believer, not self-made virtue

scripture_references.connection: David asks God for a clean heart, renewed spirit, restored joy, and sustaining grace. This closely parallels the prayer’s desire for inner cleansing that leads to renewed delight in God.

Paul teaches that grace trains believers to renounce ungodliness and become a people zealous for good works. This supports the prayer’s hope that grace will not be dimmed but will produce visible uprightness.

The blessing of Moses calls God the helper and refuge of Jeshurun, a name associated with Israel as God’s upright people. This illuminates the original closing phrase and the prayer’s praise of God as the one who enables uprightness.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The prayer gives thanks for unanswered prayer and for affliction as divine discipline. This can be pastorally sensitive, especially for readers in severe suffering; the adaptation preserves the theology while avoiding any implication that all suffering can be simplistically explained or that pain is good in itself.

The phrase “sanctified affliction” reflects a Puritan emphasis on God using trials to purify believers. This is biblically supportable but must be distinguished from seeking suffering for its own sake or treating suffering as automatically sanctifying apart from God’s grace.

The original’s “God of Jeshurun” is biblically rich but unfamiliar to many modern readers. It refers to a poetic name for Israel connected with uprightness, not to a separate title commonly used in contemporary prayer.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered “failure to find thy mind in thy Word” as opening Scripture without truly wanting God’s mind, to preserve the moral and relational force rather than making it sound like mere difficulty understanding the Bible.
I interpreted “passions of the flesh” and “lustings of the mind” broadly as bodily cravings and restless inward desires, since the original appears to include more than sexual temptation alone.
I retained the Egypt/wilderness image because it is concrete and central to the original movement: God’s painful refusal may be mercy when the heart wants a return to old bondage.

I translated the closing “God of Jeshurun” as “the God who helps your people walk uprightly,” while also supporting it with a Scripture reference, so the biblical allusion remains intelligible without requiring the reader to know the term.
